\chapter{Please}
\label{ch:te-please}
\hlchaptermodality{8}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say please in Telugu, and use the polite -aṇḍi verb ending speakers actually reach for.}

Build \te{దయచేసి} out of daya (\textquotedblleft{}compassion\textquotedblright{}) + cēsi (\textquotedblleft{}having done\textquotedblright{}), then make the everyday polite request instead: \te{కూర్చోండి}, \textquotedblleft{}please sit.\textquotedblright{}
\end{chapteropening}

\section[dayacēsi]{\te{దయచేసి} (dayacēsi) — please (having done compassion)}

\label{lesson:TE-C08-dayachesi}



\begin{quote}
Telugu's \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{} carries a whole small sentence inside it: \textquotedblleft{}having \textbf{done} (me) a compassion.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The word}
\textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} = \textbf{please}, literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{having done kindness / compassion}.\textquotedblright{} Two pieces:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{దయ}} (\emph{daya}) = \textbf{compassion, kindness, grace} — from Sanskrit \textbf{daya}.
  \item \textbf{\te{చేసి}} (\emph{cēsi}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{having done},\textquotedblright{} from the verb \textbf{\te{చేయు}} (\emph{cēyu}) \textquotedblleft{}to do.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

So \emph{dayacēsi} is \emph{having done (a) kindness} — you ask by crediting the listener with the grace you hope they'll show.

It is the twin of \textbf{Tamil} \emph{tayavu seytu} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{do} the kindness\textquotedblright{}) — both use a \textquotedblleft{}do\textquotedblright{} verb — and cousins with \textbf{Kannada} \emph{dayaviṭṭu} (\textquotedblleft{}having \textbf{placed} compassion\textquotedblright{}). Further off, \textbf{Arabic} \emph{min faḍlik} (\textquotedblleft{}from your \textbf{grace}\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{Hindi} \emph{kṛpayā} (from \emph{kṛpā}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{compassion}\textquotedblright{}) ask in the very same spirit.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{daya} + a light verb, four ways:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Telugu \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} \emph{daya\textbf{cēsi}} — compassion \textbf{+ having done}
  \item Tamil \textbf{\ta{தயவுசெய்து}} \emph{tayavu \textbf{sey}tu} — kindness \textbf{+ do}
  \item Kannada \textbf{\ka{ದಯವಿಟ್ಟು}} \emph{daya\textbf{viṭṭu}} — compassion \textbf{+ having placed}
  \item Malayalam \textbf{\ml{ദയവായി}} \emph{daya\textbf{vāyi}} — compassion \textbf{+ as / having become}
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Honestly: the standalone word is somewhat \textbf{formal / emphatic}. Day-to-day, Telugu politeness rides on the \textbf{respectful command} ending \textbf{‑\te{ండి}} (\emph{-aṇḍi}): \textbf{\te{కూర్చోండి}} (\emph{kūrcōṇḍi}) \textquotedblleft{}please sit,\textquotedblright{} \textbf{\te{చెప్పండి}} (\emph{ceppaṇḍi}) \textquotedblleft{}please tell me.\textquotedblright{} That \emph{-aṇḍi} is already \textquotedblleft{}please.\textquotedblright{} Put \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} in front to warm it further.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: Sound \& structure point}
The middle syllable \textbf{\te{చే}} is \emph{ca} wearing the \textbf{long‑ē} sign \textbf{‑\te{ే}} (the counterpart of the short‑e sign \textbf{‑\te{ె}}), giving \emph{cē}; then \textbf{\te{సి}} is \emph{sa} + the \emph{i} sign (\textbf{‑\te{ి}}). Telugu marks a vowel's length and quality by the little sign riding on the consonant — the consonant stays put, the vowel-sign changes the tune.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}daya\textquotedblright{} — compassion — then \textquotedblleft{}cēsi,\textquotedblright{} having done
  \item the whole word — \textquotedblleft{}dayacēsi\textquotedblright{} = please
  \item the everyday way — the verb ending: \textquotedblleft{}kūrcōṇḍi\textquotedblright{} = please sit
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the Telugu word for please? (\textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} \emph{dayacēsi}.) What do its pieces mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Compassion}\textquotedblright{} \emph{daya} + \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{having done}\textquotedblright{} \emph{cēsi}.) Which cousins ask the same way? (\textbf{Tamil, Kannada, Malayalam} with \emph{daya} — plus \textbf{Arabic} \emph{faḍl}, \textbf{Hindi} \emph{kṛpā}.) What carries \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{} in ordinary speech? (\textbf{The respectful verb ending ‑\te{ండి}} \emph{-aṇḍi}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ka]{\te{క} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S03-letter-ka}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{◌ు} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{క}}
\textbf{\te{క}} — \emph{ka}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{k}, it is \textbf{ka}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{క} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{నమస్కారం}} \emph{namaskāram} — hello / greetings (namaskāram — \textquotedblleft{}a making of a bow\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\te{రేపు} \te{కలుద్దాం}} \emph{rēpu kaluddām} — see you tomorrow
  \item \textbf{\te{మళ్ళీ} \te{కలుద్దాం}} \emph{maḷḷī kaluddām} — we'll meet again
  \item \textbf{\te{నాకు} \te{తెలుగు} \te{వచ్చు}} \emph{nāku telugu vaccu} — 'I know Telugu'
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{క} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{క} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \te{క} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{నమస్కారం}  ·  \te{రేపు} \te{కలుద్దాం}  ·  \te{ధన్యవాదములు}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{క} three times, saying \emph{ka} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \te{క} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{క}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ka}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
